title: Spatial Coherence in Optics
short_intro: Spatial coherence is a measure of the correlation of the phase of an electromagnetic wave at different points in space transverse to the direction of propagation. It determines the ability of a wavefront to exhibit well-defined interference patterns when sampled at separated locations.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Basic understanding of wave fronts, phase difference, conditions for sustained interference, and Young's double-slit experiment requirements.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Quantitative treatment of transverse coherence length, Van Cittert-Zernike theorem, mutual coherence function, and finite source size effects on fringe visibility.

concept_notes.heading: Definition and Physical Origin of Spatial Coherence
bullets: Spatial coherence evaluates the cross-correlation of optical fields at two distinct points separated transversely at the same instant in time.
It arises fundamentally from the spatial extent of the light source; extended sources produce independent emission centers that wash out interference fringes.
A point source at infinity or an infinitely small pinhole theoretically yields perfect spatial coherence across the entire transverse plane.

concept_notes.heading: Transverse Coherence Width
bullets: The transverse coherence width (or length) l<sub>c</sub> defines the maximum spatial separation between two points in the wavefront over which the phase remains correlated.
It is inversely proportional to the angular size subtended by the source at the observation plane.
For a quasi-monochromatic source of size s at a distance R, the transverse coherence length is approximately given by l<sub>c</sub> ≈ λR / s.

concept_notes.heading: Degree of Spatial Coherence and Visibility
bullets: The complex degree of spatial coherence γ<sub>12</sub>(τ) quantifies the fringe visibility in a double-slit arrangement.
Fringe visibility V is defined as (I<sub>max</sub> - I<sub>min</sub>) / (I<sub>max</sub> + I<sub>min</sub>), which directly equals the magnitude of the complex degree of coherence |γ<sub>12</sub>|.
When |γ<sub>12</sub>| = 1, the source is completely spatially coherent; when |γ<sub>12</sub>| = 0, the source is completely spatially incoherent.

concept_notes.heading: Role of Apertures and Spatial Filtering
bullets: Placing a narrow pinhole in front of an extended incoherent source spatially filters the light, increasing the spatial coherence of the transmitted beam.
According to the Van Cittert-Zernike theorem, the spatial coherence function of an incoherent source is the Fourier transform of the source intensity distribution.
Laser sources exhibit extremely large spatial coherence due to stimulated emission and resonant cavity transverse mode selection.

derivations.title: Transverse Coherence Width from an Extended Source
derivations.conditions: Quasi-monochromatic extended source of width s, observed at distance R through two slits separated by distance d.
steps: Consider two infinitesimal elements of an extended source separated by distance x that emit light independently.
The phase difference introduced at the two observation points (separated by d) due to the displacement x of the source element is given by dφ ≈ (2π / λ) (xd / R).
Interference fringes due to different source elements wash out when the phase difference reaches 2π, which defines the limiting separation d<sub>max</sub> = l<sub>c</sub> ≈ λR / s.

derivations.title: Visibility and Complex Degree of Coherence
derivations.conditions: Two-beam interference with electric field amplitudes E<sub>1</sub> and E<sub>2</sub>.
steps: The total intensity is expressed as I = I_1 + I_2 + 2 sqrt{I_1 I_2} Re{gamma_{12}(	au)}, where γ<sub>12</sub> is the complex degree of coherence.
For equal intensity beams (I<sub>1</sub> = I<sub>2</sub> = I<sub>0</sub>), the maximum intensity is 4I<sub>0</sub>(1 + |γ_12|) and minimum intensity is 4I_0(1 - |γ_12|).
Substitute I<sub>max</sub> and I<sub>min</sub> into the visibility formula V = (I<sub>max</sub> - I<sub>min</sub>) / (I<sub>max</sub> + I<sub>min</sub>).

graphs_and_experiments.title: Young's Double-Slit Experiment with Extended Source
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A source of width s illuminating two pinholes separated by d, projecting interference fringes on a screen where visibility decreases as d exceeds l<sub>c</sub>.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates that fringe contrast (visibility) drops to zero when the separation between pinholes exceeds the transverse coherence length of the illumination.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Tested conceptually and numerically in PGT/TGT regarding fringe disappearance conditions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Visibility vs. Slit Separation Graph
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A curve plotting fringe visibility V (y-axis from 0 to 1) against slit separation d (x-axis), showing a decaying oscillatory or monotonic decrease depending on source profile.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: As the distance between the two sampling points increases, the spatial correlation decreases, resulting in washed-out interference fringes.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Interpreting graphs of visibility to determine coherence width or source dimensions.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Spatial Filtering Setup (Michelson stellar interferometer principle)
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: Light from an extended star passing through two movable mirrors/apertures, producing fringes whose disappearance measures stellar angular diameter.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Utilizes spatial coherence measurement to determine astronomical object dimensions.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Application-based questions in PGT physics regarding stellar diameter measurement.

solved_numericals.question: Light of wavelength 600 nm from a narrow slit is used in a double-slit setup. If the source width is 0.2 mm and placed at a distance of 1 m from the slits, calculate the maximum slit separation for which interference fringes can be observed.
solution_steps: Identify given values: λ = 600 nm = 6 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m, R = 1 m, s = 0.2 mm = 2 × 10<sup>-4</sup> m.
Use the formula for maximum transverse coherence length: d<sub>max</sub> = λR / s.

solved_numericals.question: In a Young's double-slit experiment, the intensity maxima and minima in the interference pattern are measured to be 9 units and 1 unit respectively. Calculate the magnitude of the complex degree of spatial coherence (|γ<sub>12</sub>|) between the two slits, assuming equal beam intensities.
solution_steps: Recall the formula for fringe visibility: V = (I<sub>max</sub> - I<sub>min</sub>) / (I<sub>max</sub> + I<sub>min</sub>).
Relate visibility to the complex degree of spatial coherence for equal beam intensities: V = |gamma_{12}|.

solved_numericals.question: A circular incoherent source of diameter 2 cm is located at a distance of 5 m from an observation plane. Using light of wavelength 500 nm, find the transverse spatial coherence radius r<sub>c</sub>.
solution_steps: Identify given parameters: source size s = 2 cm = 0.02 m, R = 5 m, λ = 500 nm = 5 × 10<sup>-7</sup> m.
Calculate the angular source size θ ≈ s / R = 0.02 / 5 = 4 × 10<sup>-3</sup> rad.
Use the coherence radius relation for a circular source: r<sub>c</sub> = 0.61 λ / θ.

assumptions_and_limitations: Quasi-monochromatic approximation: Bandwidth Δν is much smaller than the central frequency ν<sub>0</sub>.
Small angle approximation is assumed in deriving transverse coherence length from source geometry.
The Van Cittert-Zernike theorem strictly applies in the Fraunhofer (far-field) diffraction regime.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Spatial coherence and temporal coherence are identical concepts.
common_misconceptions.correct: Spatial coherence refers to phase correlation across transverse spatial points, whereas temporal coherence refers to phase correlation at different times along the propagation axis.
common_misconceptions.why: They depend on different physical properties of the source: spatial coherence relates to source transverse size, while temporal coherence relates to spectral bandwidth.

common_misconceptions.wrong: An ordinary incandescent bulb has high spatial coherence.
common_misconceptions.correct: An incandescent bulb has very low spatial coherence due to its large, independent thermal emission centers.
common_misconceptions.why: Spatial coherence is inversely proportional to source size; large extended sources destroy spatial phase correlation.

quick_revision: Spatial coherence measures phase correlation across transverse points on a wavefront.
Transverse coherence length is given by l<sub>c</sub> ≈ λR / s.
Fringe visibility V equals the magnitude of the complex degree of spatial coherence |gamma_{12}|.
Spatial filtering using a pinhole increases spatial coherence by reducing the effective source size.
